books.section: The New Left, Feminism, and the Counterculture

source: original; stimulus is a licensed photograph viewed before writing (see figures) with an original account drawn from the grounding books

stimulus.source_note: Photograph: Hippies on Haight Street, San Francisco, printed in The Greenville News, April 30, 1967, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons. Account drawn from the grounding books; Leary’s phrase and the Human Be-In date verified against Smithsonian Magazine.
stimulus.text:
The photograph, printed in The Greenville News on April 30, 1967, shows young people on Haight Street in San Francisco. Some walk along the sidewalk in tight pants, boots, and sandals, with long hair and beads; others lounge against shopfronts. The printed caption calls them ‘typical hippies’ of the Haight-Ashbury district.

In 1967, the Haight-Ashbury neighborhood became a gathering place for hippies, and the ‘Summer of Love’ drew thousands of young people to San Francisco. The counterculture rejected the materialistic conformity many young people had grown up with in the 1950s. Hippies lived communally, experimented with psychedelic drugs such as LSD, and gathered at ‘be-ins’ in Golden Gate Park. At the Human Be-In on January 14, 1967, Timothy Leary urged the crowd to ‘Turn on, tune in, drop out.’

stem: The photograph best shows which feature of hippie life in Haight-Ashbury?

options.text: Its members wore business suits and ties to their office jobs
options.misconception: The photograph shows casual dress and long hair, not business suits.

options.text: Its members lived only in rural farming communes
options.misconception: Haight-Ashbury was a city neighborhood, not only a rural commune.

options.text: Its members avoided San Francisco entirely
options.misconception: The photograph was taken in San Francisco, the heart of the scene.

options.text: Its members used dress and hair to mark themselves apart

rationales.A: The photograph shows tight pants, boots, sandals, and long hair, not business suits and ties.
rationales.B: The photograph shows young people on a city street in San Francisco, not only on rural farms.
rationales.C: The photograph was taken on Haight Street in San Francisco, the center of the scene.
rationales.D: The photograph shows long hair, beads, sandals, and tight pants, a look that marked its wearers as apart from mainstream life.
rationales.general:
1. Look at the clothes: tight pants, boots, sandals, long hair, beads.
2. Background: Nothing here matches the business dress of mainstream 1950s life.
3. The caption calls them ‘typical hippies’ of Haight-Ashbury.
4. Dress that breaks the rules is a visible way to reject the rules.
Remember: A look can be a protest: it tells the world which values you refuse.
